evals.prompt: Use /start-discovery with the attached concept note. Begin the greenfield discovery conversation; do not jump to a product specification.
evals.expected_output: Claude begins with a contextual interview turn grounded in the sponsor's real commercial workflow rather than a questionnaire. It briefly frames why the last real missed-expansion episode matters, offers one broad invitation, adds a few related prompts about the trigger, investigation, people involved, workarounds, and outcome, and explicitly invites a free-form response rather than requiring every prompt to be answered. It treats Salesforce, Snowflake, and firmographic data as dependencies, delays integration design until the opportunity is clearer, and later uses bounded platform research to unlock sharper interview topics about authority, reconciliation, timeliness, visibility, and ownership. It distinguishes sponsor belief from seller or manager evidence and maintains a durable notebook with the next context-rich interview opening. At conclusion, it creates the Greenfield Discovery Brief, an editable overview flowchart of the core value journey from a commercial signal through investigation and seller action to a meaningful outcome, and a product discovery briefing. The flow marks what the proposed product must make happen and where Salesforce, data providers, managers, or sellers own a handoff. It adds focused branch flows only where the multi-actor and multi-platform context would make the overview unclear. Supporting visuals explain actors, opportunity, dependencies, and learning priorities without presenting a target architecture. Its questions and artifacts use familiar words and do not expose process jargon.

evals.prompt: Run /start-discovery on this greenfield consumer application idea. Help me develop it, but keep the conversation natural.
evals.expected_output: Claude preserves the AI meal-planning idea without accepting its framing and opens a natural interview about one recent meal-planning episode. It sets context, invites the participant to tell the whole story, and offers a few optional prompts covering coordination, shopping, decisions, failure, workarounds, and household actors without turning them into a checklist. It treats the claim that recommendations are the main unmet need as a hypothesis. It delays product recommendations until a target opportunity is clear and uses context-rich interview turns in plain, conversational English. At conclusion, it creates one compact core value journey flowchart from the household trigger through coordinated decisions and preparation to the meaningful meal outcome. It makes the proposed product's responsibility and household handoffs clear, then contracts the rest of the artifact set to the brief, only useful supporting visuals, and one concise discovery briefing rather than manufacturing enterprise-system diagrams.

evals.prompt: Use /start-discovery to develop this regulated workflow idea. We need both product and technical discovery, but no architecture yet.
evals.expected_output: Claude first uses a contextual, open-ended interview turn to clarify the real vendor-onboarding workflow and jurisdiction before researching public regulatory facts. It keeps bank policy and acceptable automation decisions with the participant, and later uses coherent scenario prompt clusters to uncover auditability, trust, human override, failure, security, and data-retention conditions without presenting a requirements checklist. It states the conditions future architecture must support without choosing a technical design. At conclusion, it creates one readable overview of the core value journey and focused flows for approval, human override, or recovery only where those branches materially change responsibility or risk. It expands the supporting visual package where the cross-functional actors, information lifecycle, responsibility boundaries, and critical assumptions need separate views. The briefing cites public regulatory research and keeps internal policy claims attributed. It does not select a target architecture. It explains uncommon regulatory or technical terms when they first appear.

evals.prompt: Resume /start-discovery from the attached notebook. Continue naturally from where we left off rather than repeating early discovery.
evals.expected_output: Claude reconstructs the current middle-discovery position, recognizes the established actors, story, and opportunity branches, does not repeat settled early questions, and assesses whether electronic health record or policy research is useful for the next phase. It opens with a plain, context-rich interview turn: a short playback of the handoff tension, why the comparison matters, a broad invitation to compare a successful handoff with one where information is lost, a few optional prompts, and permission to answer freely or correct the framing.
